parts.title: How I became a cartoonist
parts.instructions: Read the article and choose the best answer for each question.
parts.passage:
When I was eleven, I was too shy to talk in class, so I started drawing small pictures in my notebook instead. My drawings were about a rabbit called Max, who gets into trouble wherever he goes. My friends loved them, and soon they were asking me for a new story every week.

Last year, my art teacher suggested that I put the comics online. I was afraid at first, because anyone in the world could see them. In the end, I made a simple website, and I wrote a short story to go with each picture. I got only five readers in the first month, and four of them were my relatives.

Then something unexpected happened. A famous cartoonist saw my comic and shared it with his followers. By the next morning, over three thousand people had visited my site. I could hardly believe it.

I am still at school, and drawing takes up many of my evenings, but I do not mind. My dream is to become a professional cartoonist, and I try to draw something every day, even when I am tired.

parts.title: How a cartoon film is made
parts.instructions: Choose the sentence that fits each gap. There are three extra sentences.
parts.passage:
Making a cartoon film takes a great deal of time and many people. [1] Writers decide what will happen and in which order, and artists make simple drawings of each scene.

Next, the artists create the characters. [2] A character must look the same from the front, from the side and from behind, so that the audience always recognises it.

Then comes the animation. In the past, artists drew thousands of pictures by hand. [3] Today, most of the work is done on computers, which saves months of effort.

Voices are recorded separately. [4] The actors often read their lines in a small room with a microphone, and they sometimes watch the drawings while they speak.

Finally, music and sound are added. [5] A single minute of a film can take several weeks to finish.
sentences: They are usually paid by the hour.
Many cartoon characters are later sold as toys.
This is often done before the pictures are finished.
A cartoon about animals needs only a few characters.
All of this work needs a lot of patience.
They try out many different faces, clothes and colours.
Each picture was only slightly different from the one before.

gaps.explanation: The story comes first; the next sentence says writers decide what will happen.
The artists create the characters and try out faces, clothes and colours; then a character must always look the same.
Artists drew thousands of pictures by hand, each slightly different, before computers.
Voices are recorded before the pictures are finished; the next sentence is about the actors.
All this work needs patience; the next sentence says one minute can take weeks.

parts.title: A short history of comics
parts.instructions: Write one word in each gap.
parts.passage: Comics have been popular [1] more than a hundred years. The first ones appeared in newspapers, where they were printed in black and white. [2] 1938, a new kind of hero appeared who could fly, and sales increased very quickly. [3] then, thousands of different characters have been created. Some stories are funny, [4] others are serious or scary. Today, many people read comics on their phones instead [5] buying them in shops. However, printed comics have not disappeared. Old copies can [6] worth thousands of pounds.

gaps.explanation: For is used with a period of time: for more than a hundred years.
In is used with a year: in 1938.
Since then means from that time until now.
The sentence contrasts two kinds of story.
Instead of is followed by the -ing form.
Can be worth: modal verb followed by the infinitive.

parts.title: A cartoon workshop
parts.instructions: Listen to the talk and complete each note. Write one or two words, a number, a date or a time.

turns.speaker: cartoonist
turns.text: Hello, everyone. My name is Olin, and I have been a cartoonist for twelve years. Before that I taught art in a school for eight years, but I always wanted to draw for a living, so one day I took the risk. Welcome to today’s workshop about drawing a funny face. Please sit at a table and take a piece of paper. Now, a lot of you have a pen in your hand. Please put it away. Beginners always think a pen looks more professional, and I did the same, but a mistake in pen can’t be fixed. Start with a soft pencil, and use an eraser as often as you like. Marker pens are for the end. Let’s talk about the eyes. If you want the face to look friendly, draw large ones. Small eyes look serious, even a bit angry. Big ears are very funny, and we’ll draw some later, but they don’t make the face friendly. Next, feelings. Most people think the mouth does all the work. It helps, of course, but the eyebrows are the real secret. Move them up and the character is surprised. Move them down and he is angry. Try it on your paper now. Then we come to the mouth. A wide smile means that the character is happy. A small, straight line means he is bored, and a downward curve is sad. Some people draw teeth, but I think it’s better to keep it simple. We’ll take a short break at half past two, with biscuits and juice in the hall. The workshop finishes at four, and you can take your drawings home. I thought about five o’clock, but the school needs the room. Don’t forget to sign the list at the door if you’d like to come next month. Right, let’s start. Pencils ready?

gaps.prompt: Olin's job as a cartoonist began ___ years ago
gaps.explanation: He has been a cartoonist for twelve years; eight years is the time that he taught art.

gaps.prompt: Begin the first lines of your drawing with a soft ___
gaps.explanation: He tells them to put the pen away and start with a soft pencil.

gaps.prompt: To make a face look friendly, draw large ___
gaps.explanation: Large eyes look friendly; small eyes look serious and big ears are only funny.

gaps.prompt: Characters show their feelings best with their ___
gaps.explanation: Most people think of the mouth, but the eyebrows are the real secret.

gaps.prompt: A character looks happy when he has a wide ___
gaps.explanation: A wide smile is happy, a straight line is bored and a downward curve is sad.
It finishes at four; five o’clock was an idea that they dropped.

parts.title: An interview with a webcomic artist
parts.instructions: Listen to the interview and choose the correct answer.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Kendal, your webcomic has thousands of readers now. How did it all begin?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: By accident, really. I wanted to win a drawing competition at school, and I did enter one, but I didn’t win, so that wasn’t it. A teacher once told me to draw more, though that’s not the reason either. The truth is I was bored in maths and history lessons, so I filled my notebooks with a little character called Pip. My friends loved him, and they asked for a new drawing every Monday, so one day I put him online. I never expected anyone else to look at it.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: How often do you post new pages?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: People think I do one every day, and I wish I could! Each page takes me about six hours, so it would be impossible. A monthly update would be too slow, and readers would forget the story. So I post twice a week, on Tuesday and Friday. I keep to that, and my readers know it.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Where do your ideas come from?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Everywhere, honestly. I don’t need to search the internet, because most of it is nonsense, and old books are lovely but not very useful for jokes. I get them on the bus, in the supermarket, or at the café. Last week a man argued with a pigeon for ten minutes, and that went straight into the comic.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: I heard that you changed the name of a character. Why?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Yes, the grandmother, Mrs Winterbottom-Hartley. It was a very long name, but that wasn’t a problem for me. My flatmate said it looked funny, but I ignored that. In the end, I changed it because readers wrote to me saying that they couldn’t pronounce it, and some didn’t like it. Now she’s Mrs Winter, which is nicer, and nobody has complained since.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: What did you do before you could draw full time?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: For four years I worked in a clothes shop. I never taught, and I didn’t travel, although I would love to see Japan one day. I drew on my breaks and late at night. It was tiring, but I’m glad I did it, because I paid my rent and kept drawing.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: What advice would you give to young artists?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Practise a little every day, even ten minutes. You don’t need an expensive teacher or fancy pens. I started with a cheap pencil and school paper. The more you draw, the faster you improve.

parts.title: Describe a photograph
parts.instructions: Look at the photograph and speak for about one minute. Describe what you can see and say what the person might be feeling.

parts.title: Talk about the topic
parts.instructions: Answer the questions. Try to give a reason or an example with each answer.

questions.prompt: Why do you think cartoons are popular with both children and adults?
Do you prefer reading a story or watching it as a film? Why?
